name: John Knox
role: Catholic priest turned Protestant preacher, minister of St Giles', Edinburgh, leader of the Scottish Reformation

died.cause: Natural causes after a stroke and long illness

summary: Scottish preacher who survived the French galleys and exile to lead the Scottish Reformation, helping bring about the 1560 break with Rome and shaping the Presbyterian Church of Scotland.

key_dates.label: Ordained a Catholic priest; works as a notary and tutor
Called to preach by the Protestant garrison of St Andrews Castle; captured by the French and sent to the galleys
Freed from the galleys; becomes a preacher in England
Appointed a royal chaplain to Edward VI
Flees England after Mary I becomes queen
Becomes minister of the English congregation in Geneva
Publishes The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women
Returns to Scotland; his sermon at Perth sparks the Protestant revolt
Reformation Parliament rejects papal authority and adopts the Scots Confession
Preaches at the coronation of the infant James VI

accomplishments.text: Led the Scottish Reformation. In 1560 the Scottish Parliament rejected the pope's authority, forbade the Mass, and adopted a Protestant confession of faith.
Co-wrote the Scots Confession (1560) with five other ministers, the confession of faith of the Church of Scotland until it was replaced by the Westminster Confession in 1647.
Co-wrote the First Book of Discipline (1560), which set out a reformed church order with kirk sessions and called for a school in every parish and care for the poor.
Served as minister of St Giles' in Edinburgh from 1559/1560 until his death, the leading pulpit of the Scottish Reformation.

As a royal chaplain to Edward VI, influenced the 1552 English Book of Common Prayer, including the "Black Rubric" explaining that kneeling at communion did not imply adoration of the bread and wine. He declined the bishopric of Rochester.
Led the English exile congregation in Geneva (1556–1559), the community that produced the Geneva Bible (1560), though he was not one of its main translators.

Wrote The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women (1558), arguing that rule by women was contrary to nature and God's law. It was aimed at Catholic queens, but it permanently angered Elizabeth I.
Argued in his Appellation (1558) and other works that subjects and nobles may resist rulers who suppress true religion.
Confronted Mary, Queen of Scots, in a series of face-to-face interviews (1561–1563), which he recorded in his History.
Wrote the History of the Reformation in Scotland, published after his death.

persecution_note: Knox was a galley slave, an exile, a man burned in effigy, an outlaw, and a defendant in a treason trial. He was never executed, and he died of natural causes in Edinburgh in 1572. His mentor George Wishart was burned for heresy in 1546.

persecution.title: His mentor George Wishart burned for heresy
persecution.summary: Knox had become a follower and bodyguard of the Protestant preacher George Wishart, famously carrying a two-handed sword before him. Wishart was arrested, tried for heresy at St Andrews, and burned there. Knox went into hiding. Protestant conspirators murdered Cardinal Beaton three months later, though Knox was not involved.

responsible.name: Cardinal David Beaton
responsible.role: Archbishop of St Andrews and papal legate; had Wishart tried and burned
responsible.jurisdiction: Archdiocese of St Andrews, Catholic Church in Scotland

persecution.outcome: Wishart was executed. Knox hid as a tutor until he joined the Protestants holding St Andrews Castle in 1547.

persecution.title: Captured at St Andrews and made a galley slave
persecution.summary: The castle at St Andrews, held by the Protestants who had killed Beaton, surrendered to a French fleet sent to aid the Scottish government. Knox was taken to France and forced to row in the French galleys for about nineteen months, which damaged his health for life.

responsible.name: Leone Strozzi
responsible.role: Commander of the French fleet that took the castle

responsible.name: Henry II of France
responsible.role: King of France; sent the fleet and held the prisoners

responsible.name: James Hamilton, Earl of Arran
responsible.role: Governor (regent) of Scotland; sought French help against the castle

persecution.outcome: Released early in 1549, probably through the intervention of Edward VI's English government.

persecution.title: Expelled from Frankfurt
persecution.summary: Among the English Protestant exiles at Frankfurt, Knox led those who wanted a simpler service than the English Prayer Book. The rival group, led by Richard Cox, gave the city magistrates passages from Knox's writings that called Emperor Charles V an enemy of Christ, which could be treated as treason in an imperial city. The magistrates told Knox to leave.

responsible.name: Richard Cox
responsible.role: Leader of the Prayer Book party among the exiles (later Bishop of Ely)

responsible.name: City magistrates of Frankfurt
responsible.jurisdiction: Free Imperial City of Frankfurt, Holy Roman Empire

persecution.title: Condemned in his absence; burned in effigy in Edinburgh
persecution.summary: During a visit to Scotland, Knox was summoned to appear before the bishops in Edinburgh, but the summons was dropped when his supporters gathered. After he returned to Geneva, the Scottish church authorities condemned him as a heretic in his absence and burned an effigy of him at the Market Cross in Edinburgh.

responsible.name: Scottish Catholic bishops
responsible.jurisdiction: Catholic Church in Scotland (primate: Archbishop John Hamilton of St Andrews)

persecution.outcome: Sentenced to death in his absence. He stayed in Geneva until 1559.

persecution.title: Declared an outlaw by the regent Mary of Guise
persecution.summary: When Knox returned to Scotland in May 1559 and his preaching set off the Protestant revolt, the regent Mary of Guise declared him a rebel and outlaw. Elizabeth I, offended by The First Blast of the Trumpet, refused to let him travel through England on his way home.

responsible.name: Mary of Guise
responsible.role: Queen regent of Scotland; outlawed him

defended_by.name: The Lords of the Congregation
defended_by.role: Protestant nobles who took up arms against the regent and protected him

persecution.outcome: The Protestant lords won with English military help after Mary of Guise's death in 1560, and Knox became the leading minister in Edinburgh.

persecution.title: Tried for treason before the Privy Council
persecution.summary: After two Protestants were arrested for disrupting a Mass at Holyrood Palace, Knox sent a letter calling Protestants to gather in Edinburgh for their trial. Mary, Queen of Scots, treated this as treason and had him tried before the Privy Council.

responsible.name: Mary, Queen of Scots
responsible.role: Queen of Scotland; brought the charge

persecution.outcome: The council acquitted him, to the queen's anger.

persecution.title: Threatened during the civil war; leaves Edinburgh
persecution.summary: In the civil war between supporters of the deposed Mary, Queen of Scots, and those of the infant James VI, Mary's party held Edinburgh Castle and the city. Knox, weakened by a stroke and a target as the king's party's leading preacher, was threatened. According to his secretary Richard Bannatyne, a shot was fired into his house. In May 1571 he was persuaded to leave for St Andrews.

responsible.name: Queen's party (Marian faction)
responsible.role: Held Edinburgh against the king's party; threatened him

responsible.name: William Kirkcaldy of Grange
responsible.role: Captain of Edinburgh Castle and leader of the Marian forces there

persecution.outcome: He returned to Edinburgh in August 1572 and died there in November.

excommunication_note: Knox was a Catholic priest who became a Protestant. The Scottish Catholic bishops condemned him as a heretic in his absence in 1556 and burned his effigy. After the 1560 Reformation, the Catholic Church had no legal authority in Scotland, and the sentence was never lifted.

excommunications.reason: Condemned in his absence as a heretic for his Protestant preaching; burned in effigy at the Market Cross, Edinburgh
excommunications.status: Never lifted; papal jurisdiction in Scotland was abolished in 1560

persecuted_others_note: Knox did not hold civil power, but he approved the killing of Cardinal Beaton in 1546 and argued in 1558 that idolaters, by which he meant those who kept the Mass, deserved death under the law of Moses. After 1560 he pressed for Scotland's laws against saying or hearing Mass to be enforced. His sermon at Perth in 1559 was followed by a crowd sacking the town's friaries, which he blamed on the "rascal multitude" while approving the removal of "monuments of idolatry."

persecuted_others.title: Approved the murder of Cardinal Beaton
persecuted_others.targets: Cardinal David Beaton, archbishop of St Andrews
persecuted_others.summary: Protestant lairds led by Norman Leslie and William Kirkcaldy of Grange killed Beaton in St Andrews Castle in revenge for the burning of George Wishart. Knox took no part in the killing, but in 1547 he joined the garrison that held the castle and later, in his History of the Reformation, described the murder as the godly deed of men moved by God, recounting it in a mocking tone.

persecuted_others.title: Appellation: idolaters should be put to death
persecuted_others.targets: Catholic clergy and others who kept the Mass
persecuted_others.summary: In his Appellation to the nobility and estates of Scotland, and the Letter to the Commonalty published with it, Knox applied Old Testament laws (especially Deuteronomy 13) to his own day, arguing that idolatry, including the Mass, was a capital crime and that nobles and people, not only princes, were bound to punish it. He did not call for any named person to be killed.

persecuted_others.title: Pressed for the penalties against the Mass to be enforced
persecuted_others.targets: Catholic priests who said Mass and those who heard it
persecuted_others.summary: The 1560 Reformation Parliament made saying or hearing Mass punishable by confiscation, then banishment, and death for a third offence. Knox preached against Queen Mary's private Mass and, at Lochleven in 1563, told the queen that if she did not enforce the law against Mass-sayers, her subjects might punish them themselves; Protestant gentry in the west had already seized priests. Later in 1563 Archbishop John Hamilton and other priests were tried and imprisoned for saying Mass. No one is known to have been executed under the act.
persecuted_others.outcome: Imprisonment of Archbishop Hamilton and several priests in 1563; the death penalty is not known to have been carried out.

sources.citation: John Knox, History of the Reformation in Scotland, ed. William Croft Dickinson, 2 vols. (London: Thomas Nelson, 1949).

Jane E. A. Dawson, John Knox (New Haven: Yale University Press, 2015).
Rosalind K. Marshall, John Knox (Edinburgh: Birlinn, 2000).
